title: OpenFeature Reference
bottom_line: When you add, debug or change feature flags through OpenFeature, in any language, Claude uses this reference to get the API right without browsing.

sections.heading: Type the command or just ask about feature flags

nodes.label: You mention OpenFeature or its parts
You want feature flags in an app

blocks.caption: Asking "which feature flag library should I use" is enough: OpenFeature is the standard answer.

terms.definition: The CNCF vendor-neutral feature-flag standard (https://openfeature.dev): a specification plus an SDK for each language.
The plug-in that connects the SDK to a flag backend such as flagd, GO Feature Flag, Flipt, Unleash, LaunchDarkly, ConfigCat, env vars or an in-memory map.
The value your code passes with every flag check. It comes back on any error, because evaluation never throws.
The optional part of the evaluation context saying who or what is being evaluated, such as a user id. Needed for deterministic percentage rollouts.
What your code tells the provider about the request: an optional `targetingKey` plus flat attributes.

blocks.text: OpenFeature is not a flag backend. You always pair the SDK with a provider.

after.label: Claude delivers
after.text: The usual causes, checked in order with the troubleshooting table. For each: how to confirm it from the evaluation details and the code change that fixes it.

blocks.caption: The example from the plugin's README.

blocks.title: The causes Claude checks, in order

steps.title: Provider not ready yet
steps.text: The provider was registered but not ready when the first evaluation ran. A fix is to register it with `api.set_provider_and_wait(...)` so it is ready before the app serves requests.

steps.title: Flag key missing
steps.text: The flag key does not exist in the provider (`FLAG_NOT_FOUND`).

steps.title: Wrong type
steps.text: The variant type does not match the getter you called (`TYPE_MISMATCH`).

blocks.text: Claude confirms each cause from the evaluation details: `reason`, `error_code` and `error_message`.

sections.heading: Claude writes flag code that stays safe when the flag system fails

cards.title: Safe default values
cards.text: The default is the value that is correct when the flag system is down.

cards.title: Evaluate per request
cards.text: Check flags where the decision is made, not at import or in a constructor.

cards.title: Wait for readiness
cards.text: Once, at startup.

cards.title: Pass a targetingKey
cards.text: For percentage rollouts and per-user targeting.

cards.title: Match getter to type
cards.text: Including int vs float.

cards.title: Use transaction context
cards.text: For request-scoped data.

cards.title: Domains or multi-provider
cards.text: When two backends coexist.

cards.title: Provider by backend
cards.text: App code stays on the OpenFeature API.

blocks.caption: Eight of the fifteen rules the skill gives Claude. Each one in full is in the list below.

blocks.title: The writing rules in full
items: Default values are the safety net. Pick the default that is correct when the flag system is down (usually the old/off behaviour); never "the value we want in prod".

Evaluate flags where the decision is made, per request, not once at import/module load or in a constructor. An early evaluation races provider init (returns the default with `PROVIDER_NOT_READY`), never picks up later flag changes, and defeats per-user targeting. Cache only deliberately, and refresh on `PROVIDER_CONFIGURATION_CHANGED`.
Wait for readiness once, at startup. Otherwise early evaluations silently return defaults with `PROVIDER_NOT_READY`.

Always pass a `targetingKey` when the flag does percentage rollouts or per-user targeting; otherwise bucketing is undefined (`TARGETING_KEY_MISSING` on strict providers). Prefer a stable id (user id / session id / hostname), not an email.
Match the getter to the flag type, including int vs float.
Request-scoped data goes in transaction context, not in a new client per request.
Use domains (named clients + named providers) or the multi-provider when two backends coexist (e.g. migrating LaunchDarkly → flagd). Don't hand-roll fallbacks.

Vendor choice is orthogonal: pick the provider by backend and keep application code on the OpenFeature API. For a self-hosted open-source backend Claude recommends flagd (see the `flagd` skill) or GO Feature Flag; for "just a REST API", the generic OFREP provider.

sections.heading: Claude debugs, tests and hardens flag code the same careful way

cards.title: Debug with details
cards.text: Read `reason` and `errorCode`, not just the value.

cards.title: Test in memory
cards.text: Use the in-memory provider.

cards.title: Shut down on exit
cards.text: So providers flush and close.

cards.title: Keep PII out
cards.text: Unless the provider is trusted to hold it.

cards.title: Cheap, safe hooks
cards.text: Hooks must not throw in `after`/`finally`.

cards.title: Web and mobile differ
cards.text: Context is set on the API.

cards.title: Say which source
cards.text: When the bundled docs are silent.

blocks.caption: The other seven rules. Each one in full is in the list below.

blocks.title: The checking rules in full
items: Debug with details, not values. `reason` + `errorCode` tell you `FLAG_NOT_FOUND` vs `TYPE_MISMATCH` vs `DEFAULT` (rule matched nothing) vs `DISABLED`. Attach the SDK's `LoggingHook` at debug level when in doubt; the SDK itself is silent by design.
Test with the in-memory provider: no network, deterministic, supports variants + context evaluators. Reset the API between tests.
Shut down on exit so providers flush events/tracking and close streams.
Keep PII out of context unless the provider is trusted to hold it; a `before` hook can strip/anonymize attributes.

Hooks must be cheap and must not throw in `after`/`finally`; an error in `before` aborts the evaluation and returns the default (spec 4.5.x). Put telemetry in `after`/`finally`, context enrichment in `before`.

Client-side (web/mobile) is different: set context on the API (`OpenFeature.setContext`), evaluation getters are synchronous against a cached bulk evaluation, and the app reacts to `PROVIDER_CONFIGURATION_CHANGED`/`PROVIDER_CONTEXT_CHANGED` to re-render.

When the bundled docs are silent or ambiguous, Claude reads the live page on https://openfeature.dev/, the spec at https://openfeature.dev/specification/, or greps the SDK source. It says which source it used and notes the version it checked, because SDK APIs are still moving (Python is pre-1.0).

sections.heading: The skill needs nothing; running its output needs an SDK and provider

cards.title: The skill itself
cards.text: No requirements, no arguments and no environment variables.

cards.title: Running what it writes
cards.text: The OpenFeature SDK for your language and a provider for your flag backend, for example flagd (covered by the sibling `flagd` plugin), OFREP or a vendor provider.

blocks.title: Environment variables
blocks.text: None are required by the skill. Providers read their own variables (for example `FLAGD_HOST`, `FLAGD_PORT`, `FLAGD_RESOLVER` for the flagd provider); these are documented in the skill's language reference files.

blocks.title: How current the knowledge is
blocks.caption: All references were distilled from local clones taken 2026-09-21. The plan is to re-run this when an SDK ships a new minor version.
